summary: Inwangsan Shelter in the Woods, a place where you can enjoy the tranquility of reading a book in the forest of Inwangsan Mountain
description: The Inwangsan Shelter in the Woods was originally one of the military guard posts built during the January 21 Incident in 1968. The Inwang 3rd Guard Post, which was the soldiers' living quarters (now the Inwangsan Shelter in the Woods), has been transformed into a public rest area by removing the reinforced concrete piloti structure and paneling and reconstructing it with a wooden architectural structure. The shelter offers both coziness and openness with its nature-friendly wooden interior and large panoramic windows that showcase the forest views of Inwangsan Mountain. It has become a popular spot for those seeking rest in nature, attracting not only hikers taking a break but also people looking for a quiet place to read and enjoy a peaceful moment in the forest.

summary: On the rear garden grounds of Changgyeonggung Palace sits Chundangji Pond
description: On the rear garden grounds of Changgyeonggung Palace sits Chundangji Pond. It is known for its beautiful nature and fall foliage. Chundangji consists of two parts. The smaller upper half is the original location of the pond, while the lower half was initially used as a naenongpo , a place for the royal court to experiment with planting crops such as rice. However, during the Japanese occupation in 1909, the naenongpo was converted into a pond. In 1986, it was renovated into a traditional Korean style. Visitors can also see the seven-story pagoda, made in 1470, sitting on the shore of the pond.

name: Hangang Art Park
summary: A beautiful interactive park and resting area for visitors to enjoy up to 37 different public art works that put an artistic spin on the Hangang River from a cultural arts perspective. Stop on by for some personal healing amid the cold, bustling life of the city in this beautifully imaginative park dedicated to the arts filled with inspiration, wonder, and enjoyment.
description: Breaking away from the common idea that the Hangang River serves as simply a place of leisure and picnicking, the Hangang Art Park aims to present the river in a much different light. Guided by the philosophy, "Hangang, art in the flow," the park seeks to create a Hangang River that gently flows along its course at the hands of artistry. In other words, the goal is to advocate the rebirth of the Hangang River park area as a place of thoughtful communication and exchange, in line with the concept of a more stimulating and impactful form of leisure that naturally melds with the "stop" and "flow" of the river body itself. The artwork found at the park was selected through a series of art competitions that featured both professional artists and artists among the public. An artwork selection committee, comprised of specialists from a variety of fields, then worked faithfully to develop and promote the chosen artwork, which the committee had selected on the basis of not only the representation of geographical characteristics, but also substance and diversity. It was through this process of selection that the artwork currently on display was chosen, all of which belong to one of the four specified themes of the park: "Lively," "Relaxed," "Inspiring," and "Secretive."

name: Naksan Park at Night
summary: See the Seoul City Wall and beautiful views of downtown Seoul at Naksan Park.
description: Naksan Park, located in Jongo-gu, is a great place to see the Seoul City Wall and take in views of downtown Seoul. The park is famous for the beauty of its nighttime views and the city wall. Seoul during the Joseon Dynasty was smaller than it is today. At the time, there were four mountains that were contained within the city limits, Naksan Mountain being one of them. Of the four mountains, Naksan was the smallest at just over 100m tall. The city wall that is along Naksan Mountain is divided by Hyehwamun Gate, Dongdaemun Gate, and Daehak-ro. For visitors that like to hike, they should take the Seoul City Wall trail from Hyehwamun to Dongdaemun or vice versa. If they prefer an easier route, they can begin the walk at Daehak-ro. Additionally, the park has been used as a filming location for many Hallyu dramas due to its beautiful scenary. Walk the old city wall and take in the beatiful twinkling lights of Seoul at Naksan Park. Frequently Asked Questions about Naksan Park How much is parking at Naksan Park? The parking fee at Naksan Park is 300 KRW per 10 minutes, and the parking can accommodate 29 cars. Since the parking lot is limited, it is recommended to inquire in advance (02-743-7985). (As of 2024) How much is the entrance fee to Naksan Park? Naksan Park is open to all and free of charge. Can I enter Naksan Park 24 hours a day? Yes. Naksan Park is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

summary: Seodaemun Independence Park is a historic cultural site comprising a range of historic monuments and buildings.
description: Seodaemun Independence Park is a park and important historic cultural site. During the Japanese colonial period, the park housed Seodaemun Prison. Japanese imperial authorities arrested and held political prisoners and independence activists here in brutal conditions before the liberation of Korea in 1945. Today, the park is home to a history museum and monuments to independence fighters. At the Seodaemun Prison History Hall, visitors can learn about the history, struggles, and sacrifices made by Koreans during the colonial era. Visitors to the park can see the historic Dongnimmun Gate (Independence Gate), Independence Hall, and the March 1st Declaration of Independence Monument. There are several memorials and statues of patriots, such as a statue of Seo Jaepil (a Korean independence activist) and the Patriot Martyrs Monument.

summary: Tapgol Park was the first modern park built in Seoul and the birthplace of the March 1st Movement against the Japanese occupation in 1919.
description: Tapgol Park was the first modern park built in Seoul and the birthplace of the March 1st Movement against the Japanese occupation in 1919. The park is home to several national treasures including Wongaksaji Sipcheungseoktap (a 10-story stone pagoda) as well as statues and monuments dedicated to various patriots and resistance members who fought for Korean independence during the Japanese occupation. It is also the place where the Declaration of Independence from Japan was read at Palgakjeong (an octagonal pavilion). The park was once home to Heungboksa, a Buddhist temple, during the Goryo Dynasty period (918-1392). The temple underwent several subsequent changes and was later rebuilt under the name Wongaksa only to be destroyed during the Joseon Dynasty when Buddhism was officially repressed. In 1897, during the reign of King Gojong, the King’s financial advisor, John McLeavy Brown, proposed turning the site into a park. This was done and Tagpol Park opened to the public in 1920.

There are a range of facilities for visitors including an exhibition hall, a hexagonal pavilion, a senior citizens' center, and sports facilities including badminton and basketball courts and several squares. Despite its modest scale, with a height of just over 100 meters, Naksan was one of the four guardian mountains, along with Bugaksan, Namsan, and Inwangsan, of the capital of the Joseon Dynasty. It took its name from the Korean words, nakta (camel) and san (mountain). In the past, the mountain was popular with yangban, the ruling class of the Joseon Dynasty, who came to see its famous sunset view. In Naksan Park, visitors can follow the walking trail along the Seoul Seonggwak (fortress wall) stretching about 2 km from Hyehwamun to Heunginjimun, the East Gate of Seoul.

name: Bosingak Pavilion (Bell Ringing Ceremony)
summary: Bosingak Pavilion is the site of the giant bell and Seoul landmark, Bosingak.
description: Bosingak Pavilion, a bell tower located in Jongno 2-ga, Jongno-gu, was the original site of the Old Bronze Bell (Treasure No.2). Due to cracks that rendered the bell unringable, it is now housed at the National Museum of Korea in Yongsan. The current bell hanging in Bosingak Pavilion is a newly cast replica, funded through public donations. It was installed on August 14, 1985, and first rung the following day, August 15. Bosingak Pavilion is renowned for hosting Korea’s iconic New Year’s Eve bell-ringing ceremony, where the bell is struck 33 times at midnight on December 31. Additionally, the bell is rung 12 times daily at noon, except on Mondays.

name: Myeongdong Cathedral
summary: Myeongdong Cathedral is the very first Roman Catholic parish church in Korea.
description: Myeongdong Cathedral is the very first Roman Catholic parish church in Korea. It is also the first Gothic building ever built in Korea and was designated as Historic site No. 285 in Korea. On the basement floor, there is a small sanctuary where the remains of the martyrs are enshrined, and where visitors to the cathedral can pay their respects. Every May, Myeongdong Cathedral holds a cultural festival. The construction of the cathedral started in 1892 and was completed in 1898. Unlike most Gothic buildings, Myeongdong Cathedral was built with bricks instead of stones. It gives the cathedral a characteristic atmosphere. The splendid high ceilings inside the church and the arches in between the magnificent inner pillars show the beautiful Gothic style well. The basement contains the remains of nine saints and martyrs, who devoted their lives to the propagation of Catholicism in Korea. Behind the cathedral, Seongmo Dongsan (St. Mary's garden) is situated. During lunch hour, pipe organs are playing here. The garden offers a peaceful resting space after visiting the cathedral.

description: Cheongwadae Sarangchae is a historical memorial museum where visitors can learn about the past, present, and future visions of Seoul and Korea. Originally the home of the public information hall of Cheongwadae (the Blue House, the Korean presidential residence) called “Hyojadong Sarangbang”, it re-opened with its present name in January 2010 after extensive renovation. Cheongwadae Sarangchae is a two-story building, with exhibition halls, souvenir shops, a resting area on the first floor, and experience zones on the second floor. Cheongwadae Sarangchae features the Korea Hall, the Hi Seoul Hall, a traditional handicrafts demonstration room, a souvenir shop, and a café on the first floor. Various cultural events, such as demonstrations of traditional handicrafts and traditional Korean tea tasting, are held regularly in the lobby. The souvenir shop stocks Cheongwadae-themed goods and traditional Korean items. After viewing the exhibitions, it is pleasant to take a break at the café and enjoy a cup of traditional Korean tea. The Presidential Hall on the second floor displays material about the former presidents of Korea. Here visitors can explore the political and economic events of Korea from the past up to the present day via pictures and visuals. Visitors can also see at a glance a chronology of the past 60 years of Korean history, as well as the major events in the democratization and industrialization of Korea.

name: Seo-Seoul Museum of Art Inaugural Special Exhibition 《Our Time Begins Here》
summary: An exhibition that illuminates the construction process of the Seo-Seoul Museum of Art and the narrative of time engraved in the southwestern region (and its people) as a 'record of memories'.
description: 《Our Time Begins Here》 is an exhibition that illuminates the construction process of the Seo-Seoul Museum of Art and the narrative of time engraved in the southwestern region (and its people) as a 'record of memories'. Through the resonance of works that reflect the scenes of West Seoul remaining amidst the processes of creation and extinction, and the time differences that occur in between using the language of art, it constructs the memories of the construction of the Seo-Seoul Museum of Art, its surrounding time, places, and community into a multi-layered structure. By weaving together the diverse layers of relationships surrounding the museum—from the people who passed through the birth of the Seo-Seoul Museum of Art together, to the region and future generations—under the name of 'us', it seeks to explore the meaning of 'time' that new media art possesses within the accumulated narratives. name: Welcome to Hanseongbu: Governing the Capital of Joseon
summary: Visit Hanseongbu, the Seoul City Hall of the Joseon Dynasty, to handle your affairs! Seoul Museum of History Special Exhibition.
description: Hanseongbu was the institution that managed the affairs of the capital, much like today's Seoul City Hall, and its head, the Panyun, oversaw the entire capital city and led its urban administration. Furthermore, it also possessed the characteristics of a central administrative agency, directly participating in state administration. Therefore, Hanseongbu was in charge of urban administration—such as household registry compilation, housing management, and the processing of various civil complaints—while concurrently undertaking nationwide duties, including maintaining order in the royal capital, storing household registries, and handling legal disputes. This exhibition comprehensively illuminates the various functions and aspects of Hanseongbu, aiming to reflect on the appearance and significance of modern-day Seoul through this historical lens. The realities of administration captured in historical records and the stories of the people who lived within those systems continue to offer valid questions and profound insights for us living today. We hope that the familiar yet unfamiliar story of Hanseongbu unfolding in this exhibition will serve as an opportunity to look anew at Seoul, the city where we work and live today.

Mandy El-Sayegh questions what the institutionalized systems of knowledge and classification systems that have defined our world have excluded and what they have naturalized. category: Culture > Cultural Facilities > Others Cultural Facilities
name: Dilkusha
summary: Dilkusha, a red-brick house signifying "a joyful heart" in Persian. A historic residence reflecting the lives of the Taylor family who built it a century ago, alongside the elegant narrative embedded
description: Dilkusha, meaning "a joyful heart" in Persian, is the historical name given to the residence of Albert W. Taylor and Mary L. Taylor. The Taylor family commenced construction in 1923 and completed Dilkusha in 1924. Following a devastating fire in 1926, the structure was rebuilt in 1930. After the Japanese colonial authorities deported the Taylor couple in 1942, the property was briefly managed by Albert's younger brother, William W. Taylor. In 1959, the house was purchased by lawmaker Cho Kyeong-kyu of the Liberal Party. However, following the forfeiture of his assets to the state in 1963, ownership of Dilkusha transferred to the government. Left neglected for decades, the property severely deteriorated and lost its original form. In 2005, Professor Kim Ik-sang of Seoile University located the estate at the request of Albert’s son, Bruce T. Taylor. In 2006, Bruce finally returned to his childhood home after 66 years, bringing Dilkusha back to public prominence.

Reborn as the Lee Hoe-young Memorial Hall, this house possesses rich historical backgrounds and values even from an architectural history perspective. To remember its significance together, the Lee Hoe-young Memorial Hall gave this old Western-style building the nickname 'The Old House on Sajik-dong Hill' while reshaping the site. Mr. Lee Hoe-young devoted himself to the anti-Japanese independence movement, contributing his entire family wealth to establish the Shinheung Military Academy. At the Lee Hoe-young Memorial Hall, encounter the history of the independence movement expressed with modern aesthetics, alongside the stories of the finest family of the Joseon Dynasty, the greatest revolutionaries of Joseon, the people who turned darkness into light, and the people who turned orchid leaves into blades.

summary: Exhibiting Gungisi relics and excavated artifacts from the Joseon Dynasty discovered during the construction process of the new Seoul City Hall.
description: During the site preparation construction process for the new Seoul City Hall in 2008, a large number of structural remains and artifacts presumed to be from the Joseon Dynasty were identified, leading to an excavation investigation. Here, various artifacts such as ceramics, coins, and roof tiles were excavated alongside structural remains like building sites and stone revetments constructed during the modern era and the Joseon Dynasty. In particular, many weapons from the Joseon Dynasty were identified, including Chongtong (gun barrels), Cheolhwan (iron cannonballs), and the Bullanggi Japo (breech-loading swivel gun) designated as a Treasure. As a result of investigating old maps and related materials, it was determined that Gungisi, a government office in charge of manufacturing weapons during the Joseon Dynasty, was located near Seoul City Hall. The Seoul City Hall site is presumed to have been part of the past Gungisi, and the Gungisi Relics Exhibition Hall was created to preserve related structural remains and exhibit excavated artifacts.

Nestled at the foot of Inwangsan Mountain, visitors can experience the serene beauty of Korean architecture and appreciate the tranquil scenery. The site of Mugyewon, known as Mugaejeongsa, was the villa of Grand Prince Anpyeong, the third son of King Sejong. Inspired by its resemblance to the utopian paradise he saw in a dream, Grand Prince Anpyeong built a pavilion where he composed poetry and practiced archery. This historically significant location is also where An Gyeon, the foremost painter of the time, created the famous "Dream Journey to the Peach Blossom Land" in just three days. Since its opening in 2014, Mugyewon has offered a variety of cultural programs, including performances, exhibitions, lectures, education, and hands-on experiences. If you wish to experience Korean tradition and culture amidst scenery as beautiful as the mythical Peach Blossom Land, we recommend visiting this place.

summary: Founded in 1978, the Kyunghee University Natural History Museum is run by the university.
description: Upon opening its doors in 1978, the Kyunghee University Natural History Museum served as a little respite of nature in the city that boasted of a collection of nearly 90,000 specimen on display. The museum was initially founded upon the purpose of realizing the Kyungee University founding ideology of "Creating a world of culture" grounded in the results that had been obtained through several years of studying nature. The effort continues to approach the distancing relationship between nature and humankind amid rapid societal changes and urbanization with a "respite of nature in the city" that provides a sense of living in harmony with nature. All six floors of the museum display easy-to-understand exhibits capturing a comparison between the current state of evolution and the process of transformation up to the present-day with specimen of different plants and animals, as well as various rocks from sedimentary to igneous and metamorphic rocks that were used for research purposes by specialized teams of professors in various fields. There are courses and tour programs offered to help understand and practice nature preservation and the importance of life within the framework of these exhibited specimen. The Kyunghee University Natural History Museum has collected numerous specimen since the 1940s, while possessing a collection of more recent domestic specimen that have already become extinct or show signs of endangerment. The museum offers the opportunity for children and adults alike to more systematically learn about the classification and ecosystems of animals and plants and prioritizes itself with the fervor of exploring nature, as well as the awareness of nature protection.

name: National Museum of Korean Contemporary History
summary: The National Museum of Korean Contemporary History houses exhibitions that spans modern Korean history, from the 19th century to today.
description: The National Museum of Korean Contemporary History houses exhibitions that span modern Korean history, from the first opening of Korea to outsiders in the late 19th century to today. The museum is the country's first national museum of contemporary history. The eight-story museum has many facilities: there are four permanent exhibition halls and two special exhibition halls, seminar rooms, lecture halls, a rooftop garden, a museum shop (that sells souvenirs), a cafe, and storage lockers. The four permanent exhibitions cover different periods of Korean history and there are over 1,500 artifacts and items here. Some of the displays are patriot Ahn Jung-Geun's last writings, the March 1st Declaration of Independence, belongings of fallen soldiers from the Korean War, and materials relating to democratic activism. The museum's first floor contains two special exhibition halls. Here, you will find a variety of limited-time exhibitions relating to Korean history, politics, society, and culture. Additionally, visitors can listen to, watch, and experience the modernization of Korea through state-of-the-art technology. There is also the Children's Museum, where children can learn and experience history for themselves with the museum’s “Our History’s Treasure Chest” area.

name: buruttrak
summary: A record shop opened in Myeong-dong in 1979.
description: Buruttrak, established in 1978, is a long-standing record shop still in operation today. Known as a landmark in Myeong-dong, it has appeared in films and dramas several times. The first floor features K-pop albums and merchandise, the second floor sells jazz and pop CDs, and the third and fourth floors are dedicated to classical vinyl records. Within the vast collection of over 100,000 records, there is a particularly large selection of classical LPs. With some luck, you might also find rare albums by American Black musicians from the 1980s and 1990s. In the 1990s, as the hobbies of the Korean public shifted, record purchases began to decline. However, Japanese LP enthusiasts started buying records at high prices. During this period, the main customer base gradually shifted to foreigners. By the late 1990s, Korean record shops became essential tourist spots for Japanese visitors who could buy K-albums cheaper than in their country. Back then, the area around Hoehyeon Underground Shopping Center and Myeong-dong had 11 record shops, with 'Buruttrak' being a well-established figure. Nowadays, with K-pop's global popularity, the shop attracts customers from Southeast Asia and Europe, and it stocks a wide variety of records to meet diverse tastes.

name: Gongneung-dong Dokkaebi Market
summary: Gongneung-dong Dokkaebi Market originated from street vendors gathered near Hwarangdae
description: The Gongneung-dong Dokkaebi Market originated from street vendors who gathered near Hwarangdae Station when the Gyeongchun Railway opened on July 25, 1939. Named for its fleeting nature, like a goblin's visit, the vendors would quickly disappear at the sign of a crackdown and reassemble snugly along the tracks to rebuild the market once things were clear. This traditional goblin market is the precursor to today's Gongneung-dong Goblin Market. Since then, the market has operated as a quintessential neighborhood market in Nowon-gu, as if a goblin's magic wand has made every possible item available. It offers a variety of products including livestock, groceries, restaurants, miscellaneous goods, and agricultural products. The market draws a steady stream of visitors due to its high-quality goods sold at affordable prices. Since 2019, it has been growing into an eastern landmark cultural tourism market, concurrent with the development of the Gyeongchun Line (Railroad) Forest.

description: Gyeongguksa Temple, nestled on the eastern slopes of Samgaksan (now known as Bukhansan), is a historic temple founded in the late Goryeo period. Renowned for its scenic mountain surroundings and fresh spring water, it attracts many visitors. The temple complex has 17 buildings, including Geungnakbojeon (Hall of Supreme Bliss), Yeongsanjeon, Myeongbujeon, Gwaneumjeon, and Sibangseonwon. Geungnakbojeon houses the Amitabha Buddha triad, along with wooden Buddhist paintings (designated as Treasure No. 748), Shinjungtaenghwa, and Palsangtaenghwa. Sibangseonwon offers a weekly Sunday meditation session, and the temple also hosts temple stay programs at Hwanheodang and Manwoldang. As one of Seoul's significant temples, Gyeongguksa was frequently visited by former President Syngman Rhee. During his tenure as Vice President, Richard Nixon of the United States visited the temple and later described it as one of his most memorable experiences in his memoirs, even including a photograph of his visit.

name: Hwagyesa Temple
summary: Hwagyesa Temple was founded by Seonsa (Seon master) Sinwol in 1522 (17th year of King Jungjong's reign).
description: Hwagyesa Temple was founded by Seonsa (Seon master) Sinwol in 1522 (17th year of King Jungjong's reign). Originally, Daesa (a high Buddhist priest) Beopin, or Tanmun, built a hermitage called Bodeokam near the site of Hwagyesa Temple, preserving long-standingBuddhist tradition. Later on, Seonsa Sinwol would move the hermitage to the current location and rename it Hwagyesa. During the Joseon Period, the royal family frequented the temple and Regent Heungseon Daewongun supported the temple during the latteryears of Joseon. A cradle of the enlightenment movement, Hwagyesa Temple produced a number of figures who embroiders the modern history of Korea, including Mubul and Cha Hong-sik, and is also known to have served as a place for monks who participated in the Gapsin Revolutionto prepare for the enlightenment movement. Hwagyesa Temple is a historic venue where the Korean Language Society organized a stay of nine Korean language scholars, including Lee Hui-seung and Choe Hyeon-bae, wherein they completed the Unified Korean Orthography in 1933. Recently, the temple becameinternationally known as being a center for worldwide propagation. In 1991, the Daejeokgwangjeon Hall was established and an international seonwoen (Seon monastery) was opened on the 4th floor to accommodate buddhists from other countries. Programs ㆍ Prayer/ceremonial offering to Buddhaㆍ Buddhist University/Citizens' Seonwoen (meditation practice)ㆍ Hwagyesa Templestay: A program to experience the temple's daily life, traditional culture of Korean Buddhism and spirit of practice while stayingin the temple

description: Yanghwajin Foreign Missionary Cemetery is the final resting place for Korea's western residents, including Dr. Horace Allen, the first director of Gwanghyewon, the first western-style hospital in Korea, founded in 1885. The cemetery is known as Foreign Missionary Cemetery because of the number of foreign missionaries buried here. Tombs and headstones were built in a western style creating an exotic atmosphere. The cemetery is located near the Hangang (River), an ideal spot for taking a pleasant stroll. Yanghwajin Foreigners' Cemetery is situated on the other side of Yanghwajin, opposite the martyrs’ shrine. It is regarded as a Protestant shrine because many Protestant missionaries are buried there. The “100th Anniversary Memorial Church” was established in Yanhwajin by the “Council for the 100th Anniversary of the Korean Church” to commemorate a century of missionary work in Korea. Many of the foreigners who have contributed to the story of modern Korean history are buried in the Yanghwajin cemetery, such as Thomas Bethell, the founder of Daehan Maeil Sinbo (Newspaper); Mary Scranton, the founder of Ewha Hakdang (a mission school for girls, now Ewha Womans University); and Henry Appenzeller, the founder of Chungdong First Methodist Church. A guided tour in English or Japanese is available in Yanghwajin Foreign Missionary Cemetery when booked in advance. These are conducted four times a day (10:00, 11:30, 14:00, 15:30) except during the New Year's holiday, Chuseok holiday and on Christmas day. Yanghwajin Foreign Missionary Cemetery is located in Hapjeong-dong, Mapo-gu. It is a haven for foreign missionaries and their families who loved, and wished to lie in, Korea. The templestay program gives an opportunity to experience everyday life in the temple, which includes traditional Korean Buddhist culture and practices. Visitors can experience some simple Buddhist practices such as the daily dawn service, Korean Zen meditation, Dado (a tea drinking ceremony), and Balwoogongyang (a Buddhist meal with traditional bowls). Every May on Buddha's birthday, Bongeunsa holds the Lotus Lantern Festival on nearby Samseong-don g.

name: Korea Central Mosque
summary: The Seoul Central Mosque was established to be a place to worship for Muslims in Korea as well as to educate the larger public about Islam and Islamic cultures.
description: Located in Hannam-dong, Yongsan-gu, Seoul, the Seoul Central Mosque is the first Islamic Mosque in Korea. It was established on May 21, 1976, after construction began in October 1974. The Korean government provided the site in May 1969 with approximately 4,958 square meters of land, and the construction costs were supported by Islamic countries worldwide, including Saudi Arabia. Situated between the Hangang River and Namsan Mountain, the mosque features prayer halls on the first and second floors, with ablution rooms for men and women in the basement of the annex building. The first floor of the annex houses classrooms, while the second floor has office spaces. The adjacent Islamic Center includes facilities such as an Islamic mission center for children, a Muslim congregation, a women's association, and a library. The exterior of the Seoul Central Mosque features a variety of amenities, including halal restaurants, a halal butcher shop, an Islamic bookstore, a halal supermarket, and a travel agency, making it convenient for Muslims and non-Muslims to visit. Sunginwon is the burial place of Crown Prince Yi Jin, grandson of King Gojong and Princess Consort Sunheon. Yeonghwiwon and Sunginwon were once known as Hongneung as Queen Myeongseong, the first wife of King Gojong was entombed here. The grave was moved to Geumgok-dong in the city of Namyangju in 1919 following the death of King Gojong. Since then, the site has been known as Yeonghwiwon and Sunginwon. Apart from its historic significance, the greenery and beautiful surroundings here have always attracted sightseers.

The ancient Hanseong Baekje Kingdom was founded along the Hangang River in 18 BCE and lasted for nearly 5 centuries. The tombs were discovered in the 1970s during the Jamsil District Zoning Project and there are 8 tombs altogether. Unfortunately, most of the artifacts were stolen at some point in time, but the tombs themselves were preserved well. Visitors can observe the original structures of the tombs and learn more about Hanseong Baekje. These ancient tombs are an important historical site and the area around the tombs was made into a park. There are paths between the tombs and visitors can take a quiet walk around the park and observe the tombs while enjoying the park's fresh air and grass. The site holds the designation of Historic Site No. 270.

summary: Sungnyemun Gate (Namdaemun) is one of Seoul's historic Four Great Gates and it was designated National Treasure no. 1 by the Korean government in 1962.
description: Sungnyemun Gate (Namdaemun) is one of Seoul's historic Four Great Gates and it was designated National Treasure no. 1 by the Korean government in 1962. Though its official name is Sungnyemun, it is also popularly known as Namdaemun Gate due to its location at what was once the southern end of Seoul. As the centuries passed, Seoul grew in size but Sungnyemun Gate has endured through the ages. Construction on the gate was started in 1395 and completed in 1398. In 1447, Sungnyemun saw reconstruction work carried out. The gate is the largest city gate with an arched entrance in the city, and atop the gate's wooden base stands a 2-story wooden structure. The gate is Seoul's oldest wooden structure but on Feb. 10th, 2008, much of the gate's wooden structure was destroyed by fire. Following several years of restorative work, Sungnyemun Gate can now be enjoyed in all its glory. ​

name: Changuimun Gate
summary: Located in Buam-dong, Changuimun Gate is one of the four minor city gates of Seoul.
description: Located in Buam-dong, Changuimun Gate is one of the four minor city gates of Seoul. It is also sometimes referred to as Bukmun (North Gate) or Jahamun. The gate was built by King Taejo, the first king of the Joseon Dynasty, when he constructed the fortifications surrounding the capital. In Korean history, Changuimun Gate is best known by Koreans as the gate that the rebellion faction used to enter Seoul in the Coup of 1623. A road was built to the west of the gate that accommodates traffic but Changuimun Gate itself is closed.

summary: A riverside trail along Jungnangcheon that is beautiful in all four seasons
description: Songjeong Jebang gil is located along Jungnangcheon, extending from Seongdong Bridge to Gwangnaru gil Jebang. It is famous as a cherry blossom viewing spot in spring, a green shaded walkway filled with cicada sounds in summer, and a colorful foliage path in autumn. It has been selected by the city of Seoul as one of the top 220 summer green roads and one of the top 93 autumn foliage roads, and is known as a walking path along the water. It is also recognized as a cherry blossom attraction and has been featured as a filming location for commercial advertisements. Enjoy a healing walk along the trail colored by the special seasonal tones of five thousand king cherry trees and ginkgo trees that create a dense woodland.

summary: A valley near Seoul accessible by subway
description: On the southwestern side of Suraksan Mountain lies the stunning Byeokun Valley. The name Byeokun Valley originates from the inscription “Byeokun Dongcheon (碧雲洞天)” carved into a rock in the valley. The name was given because the spectacular white rock formations of Suraksan, exposed throughout the valley, blend with the ravine’s scenery in a way that resembles white clouds resting in the area. For those who enjoy hiking, a recommended course begins at Byeokun Valley and leads up to the summit of Suraksan. For those who prefer valleys over hiking, a well-maintained wooden deck along the stream provides a refreshing spot for a picnic.

description: Anyangcheon Stream is a tributary of the Han River that flows through Anyang-si, Gwangmyeong-si, and the Seoul districts of Geumcheon-gu, Guro-gu, Yangcheon-gu, and Yeongdeungpo-gu, eventually joining the Han River west of Seongsandaegyo Bridge. Strolling along the Yangcheon Dulle-gil trail, you’ll discover a variety of charming sights and attractions. Highlights include the Anyangcheon Stream Embankment Cherry Blossom Road, the longest cherry blossom path in Seoul, as well as peaceful spaces like the Ecological Park, Family Garden, and Sports Park. In particular, you can enjoy seasonal scenery in the heart of the city along the Anyangcheon Stream : the Autumn Foliage Road (Anyangcheon Walkway) between Yangpyeong Bridge and Mok-dong Bridge, the Cherry Blossom Road between Mok-dong Bridge and Omokgyo Bridge, and the Anyangcheon Stream Ecological Plants Center between Sinjeonggyo Bridge and Ogeumgyo Bridge.

name: Eungbongsan Mountain
summary: A low mountain located in Eungbong-dong, Seongdong-gu
description: Eungbong-dong, located in Eungbong-dong, Seongdong-gu, stands at about 95 meters and has long been renowned for its beautiful scenery. During the Joseon Dynasty, kings would release hawks here for hunting, which earned it the nickname Maebongsan Mountain (Hawk Mountain). The area was also home to Dongho Dokseodang, an educational site for scholars and pavilions like Hwanghwajeong and Yuhajeong. To the south of Eungbong was a storage facility for ice called Dongbinggo. Today, Eungbongsan is designated as a neighborhood park, attracting many visitors who enjoy Seoul’s sunsets and night views. The park also offers recreational facilities such as a children's park, rock climbing area, and badminton courts, making it an excellent spot for various activities.

name: Jungnangcheon Stream Embankment
summary: Jungnangcheon Stream, a green shelter in the city where humans and nature coexist
description: In spring, the embankment of Jungnangcheon Stream is covered with canola flowers. The 5.15-kilometer section from Jangpyeonggyo Bridge to Wolleunggyo Bridge is a land of bright yellow flowers. In the summer, you can see a colorful tunnel of 40,000 roses, and in autumn, silver grass, reeds, cosmos, and sunflower flower paths create a unique autumn scenery. If Jungnangcheon is famous for its spring, summer, and autumn flowers, winter is definitely the time for migratory birds. The 3.3-kilometer section where Jungnangcheon Stream joins the Hangang River from the confluence of Cheonggyecheon Stream and Jungnangcheon Stream is a protected area for migratory birds and is perfect for sightseeing. More than 4,000 birds of more than 40 species, including herons, herring gulls, and cormorants, fly in, and 21 species of migratory birds, such as mallards and kestrels, visit especially in winter. When migratory birds visit in winter, a birdwatching program and a migratory bird observation class also take place, making the place an ecological learning center for children.

name: Kkummaru(Dream Park) in Children's Grand Park
summary: A Place Where the Past, Present, and Future of Seoul Coexist, Kkummaru(Dream Park) in Children's Grand Park
description: This park, filled with thedreams and hopes of childhood, is actually a place that holds a painfulhistory. This place was originally where the tomb of Empress Sunmyeong, thewife of Sunjung, the last king of the Joseon Dynasty, was enshrined. However, the tomb was moved to another location during the Japanese occupation, while a golf course was built for the Japanese and remained even after liberation. Kkummaru (Dream Peak) in Children's Grand Park was Korea's first "clubhouse" for tourist visiting Korea. After the opening ofChildren’s Grand Park, Kkummaru wasused for different purposes such as an academic hall, exhibition space, andsuperintendent’s office. Later, Kkummaru was able torecover its original structure that was iconic of Korea’s modern andcontemporary architecture through the hands of famous renovation architects,Cho Sung-ryong and Choon Choi. They erased the superimposed layers and filledthe building with programs for a book cafe and picnic area to reintroduce it asa space to help children dream again, hence the kkum (dream) part of the name.

name: Yongsan Park Partially Open Site
summary: The site was a previous residence for US military officers. It was named 'Sobinggo' during the Joseon Dynasty because ice was stored nearby.
description: The site was a previous residence for US military officers. It was named Sobinggo during the Joseon Dynasty because ice was stored nearby. It is now called Yongsan Garrison, including the site of the U.S. Army officers' quarters. Still, the American soldiers stationed in Yongsan right after the defeat of Japan did not call it Yongsan Garrison but Camp Sobinggo. From the Liberation to the Korean War, it was called Camp Sobinggo, but after the ceasefire agreement was reached, it was named Yongsan Garrison when the 8th US Army moved in.

This makes Baengnyeonsan mountain a great place for an easy and comfortable hike! Few Seoul residents know about this place, so unlike other mountains and trails in Seoul, there aren't too many people here. name: Ansan Mountain
summary: Ansan Mountain is 295.5 meters high and it is located in the Seodaemun-gu district of Seoul.
description: Located in the Seodaemun-gu district of Seoul, Ansan Mountain is 295.5 meters high and is popular for its easy hiking trails and beautiful scenery. While there are multiple paths to choose from, the trail on the eastern side of the mountain is the most well-known as it passes by Independence Park, the location of the historic Seodaemun Prison. Many of the paths up the mountain are made up of a boardwalk, so anyone of any age can make this trek without worrying about slipping or tripping. At the top of Ansan is an observation deck with a jaw-dropping view of Seoul and the surrounding area. Additionally, Bongwonsa Temple, which is the head temple of the Taego Order of Korean Buddhism, is located at the bottom of the southeastern hillside of the mountain.

description: The lengthy trail taking a wide sweep around Namsan Mountain while being known for its particularly scenic landscape during the autumn season, earned the name, "Autumn Trail" some years ago. There are a total of four distinct courses, including Namsan Southern Walking Path, Namsan Northern Walking Path, Sowol-ro, and Namsan Outdoor Botanical Garden. Also known as "Itaewon-ro," the Namsan Southern Walking Path is filled to the brim with striking Oriental Plane trees makng for an amazing vista of autumn foliage! It spans a total of 1.3 km from Namsan National Theater Intersection to the Namsan 3-ho Tunnel and is at the peak of fall viewing from late October to early November.

Featuring wide grassy fields perfect for picnics, a bike path stretching all the way to Banpo District, and also a tennis court for the disabled, Jamwon Hangang Park continues to attract many visitors. From the Joseon Dynasty to the Japanese Occupation, the area of Jamwon-dong was a large-scale mulberry field. To educate future generations about the history of this area, Seoul Metropolitan Government opened up a "Jamwon Nature Learning Center." The learning center consists of a lobby, silkworm exhibition hall, wildflower garden, and classrooms, offering various experience programs for children.

summary: A valley with cool, clear water, Uidong Valley is located between Dobongsan Mountain and Bukhansan Mountain.
description: The Ui-dong Valley, a notable valley in Gangbuk, is situated between Dobongsan and Bukhansan mountains. It features scattered waterfalls and ponds, with a long stream flowing from the entrance to Baegundae, the gentlest course in Bukhansan Mountain. While swimming is prohibited due to its location within Bukhansan National Park, simply sitting on a rock and breathing in the refreshing air is enough to beat the heat. summary: Cheonggyecheon Stream is a 11-km long stream that runs through downtown Seoul, created during an urban renewal project.
description: Cheonggyecheon Stream is an 11 km-long stream that runs through downtown Seoul. Created as part of an urban renewal project, Cheonggyecheon Stream is a restoration of the stream that was once there during the Joseon Dynasty (1392-1910). The stream was covered with an elevated highway after the Korean War (1950-1953), as part of the country's post-war economic development. Then in 2003, the elevated highway was removed to restore the stream to its present form today. The stream starts from Cheonggye Plaza, a popular cultural arts venue, and passes under a total of 22 bridges before flowing into the Hangang River, with many attractions along the way. Cheonggyecheon’s turbulent history is on display at the Cheonggyecheon Museum, which opened in September 2005. The museum offers visitors the chance to learn about the many changes the stream has seen, including being buried underground and being restored. The story is told with the help of a scale-model and period photographs. Frequently Asked Questions about Cheonggyecheon Stream Is the Cheonggyecheon Stream promenade always open? Yes. The Cheonggyecheon Stream promenade is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. However, in the case of rain, access may be restricted for safety reasons. What festivals are held at the Cheonggyecheon Stream? The "Seoul Lantern Festival" is held annually at the end of the year around the Cheonggyecheon Stream area. (As of 2026) What is the nearest subway station to Cheonggyecheon Stream? There are a total of 11 subway stations connected to Cheonggyecheon Stream: City Hall Station (Subway Line 1, 2), Jonggak Station, Jongno 3-ga Station, Jongno 5-ga Station, Dongdaemun Station, Dongmyo Station, Sinseol-dong Station (Subway Line 1), Eulji-ro 1-ga Station, Eulji-ro 3-ga Station, Eulji-ro 4-ga Station, Dongdaemun History and Culture Park Station, Yongdu Station (Subway Line 2).

name: Bamseom Island
summary: An island located downstream of the Mapodaegyo Bridge on the Hangang River, where the Seogangdaegyo Bridge passes through
description: Bamseom is an island located downstream from Mapodaegyo Bridge on the Hangang River, intersected by Seogangdaegyo Bridge. Known as a habitat for migratory birds, Bamseom gets its name from its chestnut-like shape. In the past, the island was inhabited. Still, during the development of Yeouido, the island was split into Upper Bamseom and Lower Bamseom after an explosion forced residents to relocate to Mapo-gu. The upper part of Bamseom, with its bay-shaped shoreline, became an important bird nesting area. Over the next 20 years, sediment from the Hangang River allowed trees and grasses to flourish, attracting birds and establishing the island as a well-known urban bird sanctuary. Bamseom Island is now approximately six times larger than it was originally. In 1999, it was designated as a Natural Ecosystem Conservation Area; in 2012, it was recognized as a Ramsar Wetland. While direct access to the island is prohibited, Bamseom Island can be viewed from Bamseom Park.

description: The Gyeongchun Line (Railroad) Forest in Gongneung-dong, Nowon-gu, Seoul, once traversed by trains bound for Chuncheon, captures a unique mix of historical and modern elements. In this area, the Gongneung-dong section has evolved into a lively area reminiscent of New York's Central Park. It is connected to the adjacent Gongneung-dong Dokkaebi Market and dotted with a growing array of cafes and pubs. Consequently, this area has earned the nickname "Gongtral Park," inspired by Gongneung-dong. It's also known as "Gyeongnidan-gil" (akin to Gyeongnidan-gil in Gongneung-dong). Traditionally, old railway lines converted into parks have their tracks removed, but what sets this place apart is the preservation of its original railway tracks.

name: Hongneung Arboretum
summary: Hongneung Arboretum is Korea's oldest arboretum and was established to support the study of Korean flora.
description: Located at the southwest side of the Cheonjangsan Mountain (Elev. 141 m) in the eastern part of Seoul, as well as serving as the grounds of Empress Myeongseong’s royal tomb, the Hongneung Arboretum is revered for its high historical, cultural, and academic value that functions as Korea's first and oldest arboretum,established to support the study of Korean flora in 1922. As such, several forestry-related studies and research projects are continually conducted, while the arboretum systematically manages as many as 2,035 species (trees: 1,224 / herbs & plants: 811) of plant genetic resources, both native and foreign to Korea. During the weekdays, the arboretum works as an ecological learning facility forchildren and students ranging from kindergarten up through university, while also remaining open every weekend for local residents as a place of learning for those interested in studying nature and learning about the environment since 1993.

name: Yongsan Park
summary: Yongsan Park is a vast green open space dotted with refreshing ponds and adorned with beautiful sculptures by world famous sculptors.
description: Yongsan Park is a vast green open space dotted with refreshing ponds and adorned with beautiful sculptures by world famous sculptors. The location of Yongsan Park has historical significance: it was once used as an American command post after the Korean War, but has now been transformed into this peaceful leisure amenity open to the public. Yongsan Park is popular with Seoul families and always filled with people. Children playing and families enjoying picnics together are common sights, especially at weekends. The sculpture park, which is attached to the main park, is famous for displaying works of art by internationally – acclaimed sculptors from Germany, Switzerland, Canada, and other countries as well as Korea. Visitors can also enjoy the pleasure of free acupressure therapy in the Barefoot Park. The site of Yongsan Park is historically significant. It was used as a base by the Japanese army during the Imjin War (1592-1598), and later by the Chinese army during the Imo Incident in 1882 (the Joseon Dynasty’s political conflict between Japan and China). After the Korean War it was occupied by the American army, who used it as a golf course. Finally, it came back into Korean hands in 1992 in the form of a public park. The original park was scaled back to accommodate the establishment of the new National Museum of Korea in 1997. Since then, Yongsan Park has become a peaceful spot where people come to relax amid the endless green.

description: Dream Forest, located in northern Seoul, is the 4th largest park in the city after Seoul Forest, Olympic Park, and World Cup Park. Neighboring six surrounding districts, including Gangbuk-gu, Seongbuk-gu, and Dobong-gu, the park was built on the site where Dreamland amusement park formerly existed. Surrounded by densely forested mountains of Byeogosan Mountain and Opaesan Mountain, Dream Forest provides a variety of attractions to visitors, together with an abundant amount of natural vegetation. The Cherry Blossom Path in the spring or the Maple Tree Forest in the fall are especially beautiful. Visitors will also find attractions designed after traditional Korean architecture such as the Wolyeongji (Moon Reflecting Pond) and the Wolgwang Falls (Moonlight Falls). At the top of the observatory, visitors are treated to a panoramic view of the whole park and a view of Bukhansan Mountain, Dobongsan Mountain and Suraksan Mountain. Dream Forest also accommodates various cultural venues. The Dream Forest Arts Center, with its Performance Hall and Concert Hall, the Sangsang Toktok Art Museum and several grassy lawns and plazas offer concerts and performances throughout the year. Several restaurants and cafes are also conveniently located within the park, making Dream Forest one of the most comprehensive parks in Seoul.

name: Seoul Forest
summary: Seoul Forest was established to satisfy people’s desire to have more green space and recreational places in the center of the city.
description: Opened in 2005, Seoul Forest is a vast urban park spanning approximately 495,868.5 square meters. It is a tranquil retreat where people of all ages can experience nature within the city. When cherry blossoms and tulips bloom in the spring, the forest is filled with families, couples, and friends enjoying outings together. In the fall, it becomes a popular spot for people to enjoy music festivals amidst the cool breeze. Even in summer and winter, Seoul Forest remains a bustling green haven whenever the weather is good.Seoul Forest has five theme parks: the Cultural and Arts Park, the Eco Forest, the Experiential Learning Park, the Wetland Eco Center, and the Hangang Riverside Park Project. The first theme park, the Cultural and Arts Park, offers a variety of leisure activities. It includes a gateball court, a forest playground, a family yard with a large lawn, a statue of a military horse, a ground fountain, and an atelier. The second theme park, the Eco Forest, is designed to recreate a natural forest where wild animals and plants can coexist. The third theme park, the Wetland Eco Center, consists of eco-friendly wellness spaces such as an environmental playground, an outdoor nature classroom, and a water purification garden. The fourth theme, the Experiential Learning Park, includes features like the Keeper's Forest, Butterfly Garden, and Insect Garden. The fifth theme, the Hangang Riverside Park Project, has the Seoul Forest Quay and bike paths. Additionally, various unique gardens like the Garden of Excitement, the Bee Garden, and the Bench Garden have been added through donations from individuals and corporations, transforming Seoul Forest into an even more attractive space each year. Frequently Asked Questions about Seoul Forest Park Can I bring my pet to Seoul Forest Park? Seoul Forest allows entry with pets, but it is important to ensure that they do not inconvenience other visitors. Please properly handle pet waste and make sure to keep them on a leash (within 2 meters) How much is parking at the Seoul Forest? name: Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education Namsan Library
summary: Seoul's first public library, the Namsan Public Library
description: Seoul's first public library, the Namsan Public Library, originally opened in 1922 as the Gyeongseong Municipal Library in Myeong-dong. Situated in the heart of Namsan, the current building was constructed in 1965 following a public design competition. It has since been recognized as a Seoul Future Heritage building. The library boasts a collection of invaluable resources, including three volumes designated as Seoul City Tangible Cultural Properties and 227 volumes of 30 registered cultural properties. With a collection of around 500,000 books, 16,000 non-book materials, and 800 serial publications, Namsan Public Library is committed to preserving and sharing knowledge. In collaboration with the National Library of Korea, it has created a digital archive of rare and valuable materials, including ancient books and East Asian texts. Additionally, the library serves as a specialized resource center for Seoul's residents, offering various programs designed to enrich their cultural and intellectual lives.

name: Changsin-Sungin Quarry Observatory
summary: In the era of Japanese colonial rule, the Changsin-dong quarry was active, and atop its peak lies an observation deck, offering breathtaking night views.
description: The quarry observatory is built atop the summit of Changsin-dong quarry, providing a panoramic view of the city and natural landscapes at a glance. During the Japanese colonial period, a quarry was located in Naksan, Changsin-dong, to supply stone for the exterior of large buildings such as the Government-General of Korea, the old Seoul Station, and the Bank of Korea. After the Korean War, the quarry's use was discontinued, but the quarry observatory was located where immigrants and refugees settled to form a village. From the quarry observatory, with nothing obstructing the view, you can enjoy the skyline of Seoul at a glance. The second floor houses a coffee shop (Café Nakta), and the third floor features an outdoor observation deck, allowing you to appreciate the scenery of Seoul's cityscape and nature from any vantage point. Especially renowned is the breathtaking view that unfolds alongside the sunset. Enjoy the best panoramic view, a reasonably priced cup of coffee, and homemade ggangjeong and Nakta rice cakes. Small music concerts featuring historical and cultural stories, exhibitions, and live guitar performances are held occasionally.

It was a quarry village in the 1960s, a wooden village in the 1970s, a sewing factory in the 1990s, and finally a sewing village in the 2000s. It is situated around the rocky cliffs once used as the nation's only quarry. Changsin-dong Cliff Village is divided into densely packed, dilapidated, aged homes built on cliffs and precipices and homes formed beneath rocky hills. *Please Note: When visiting, please refrain from making excessive noise, as actual residents live there.

description: Nowhere exudes more local and traditional charm than Insa-dong, a quaint neighborhood in the center of Seoul that transports visitors back to a time when women wore hanbok and men rode horses. With its wooden tea houses, boutique galleries and street vendors selling traditional snacks, a stroll through Insa-dong is mandatory for all visitors, especially on Sundays when the streets become traffic free and come alive with street performances, buskers and throngs of young and old who have come to experience one of Seoul’s most fascinating and creative neighborhoods. While the entertainment here is free, Insa-dong is also one of the best places in Seoul to purchase traditional Korean art, products, and other souvenirs, as it is filled with antique shops, art galleries, traditional stationery shops, handicraft shops, pottery and porcelain shops, bookstores, and art supply stores. name: Hongdae
summary: Lit up by neon signs that buzz late into the night, evenings in Seoul have a creative energy that sucks people in crowds.
description: Hongdae is the scene where Korean culture, both pop and indie, manifests, especially at night. More information on planning a Sangam day trip can be soon found at K-stars and their K-style if the Korean Wave has washed over you, then there’s no better place to tread the path of such tastemakers as Hongdae, the live-wire district of music and art culture. Whether you’ve come on your own or with equally eager friends, the ever-trending university area remains the only place in Seoul where you can transitionfrom daytime exploring to nighttime adventures just as easily as you shuffle through your K-Pop playlist. Shopping in Hongdae Across the street and around the corner is a three-story store aptly named Around the Corner, Its multi-designer displays only cover two floors, but the smaller selection gives customers room to consider the subtler hip-hop motifs and mixed prints that punctuate the street wear-filled racks. Remember, just because Hongdae is more casual and “free” than, say, Gangnam or Apgujeong, doesn’t mean fashion doesn’t matter. The vibe you can see from the stores and the people on the streets, is effortless withan edge of the true Hongdae touch. You can see more of that in the quintessential Hongdae institution Aland, and the up-and-coming company Underst ar.

name: Itaewon
summary: Located smack-dab in the center of Seoul, Itaewon is home for the majority of expats that reside in Korea, making Itaewon a mini melting pot of cultures and religions from all over the world.
description: Korea is one of the most ethnically homogeneous countries in the world, but you'd never know that walking down the streets of Itaewon. Located smack-dab in the center of Seoul, Itaewon is home for the majority of expats that reside in Korea, making Itaewon a mini melting pot of cultures and religions from all over the world. The Seoul Central Mosque is also located in Itaewon along with a number of halal food stores, and large numbers of US military personnel can be seen here as the Yongsan Garrison that is stationed nearby. Due to the area’s diverse inhabitants, Itaewon has become one of the most cosmopolitan areas in Seoul boasting restaurants, shopping and nightlife that are equally diverse and cater to international tastes, attracting many other foreigners and tourists. It is safe to say that Itaewon is almost better known by foreigners and non-Korean residents than Koreans. Itaewon is known as the place to go when you want to get your foreign food fix. Restaurants featuring cuisine from all over the world can be found here including Indian, Thai, Pakistani, Greek, German, French, Italian, Australian, English, American, and Mexican, cuisines which are not easily found in Korea. Itaewon is also famous for its nightlife. Among foreigners, it is often considered the most popular area of Seoul for bars and clubs other than Hongdae. A range of drinking establishments can be found here including pubs, wine bars, hip-hop clubs, salsa clubs, lounges and cafes. Most stores in Korea offer clothing that fit Asian builds well but are unfortunately too small to fit those with “Western builds”. This leaves many of those with bigger and taller builds struggling to find clothing that fit. Fortunately many of the stores in Itaewon offer imported clothing in sizes that are difficult to find elsewhere in Korea. And if you still can’t find what you want, experienced tailors can create customized clothing. Itaewon also specializes in leather and fur goods, luggage and handbags, as well as jewelry and antique furniture. Trinkets and souvenirs can also be found here. Itaewon boasts some 100 antique stores clustered together on a single street. Originally these stores only dealt with second-hand U.S. Army furniture, but nowadays the selections at the stores have expanded to include antique furniture from around the world. These are the following tourist attractions around Itaewon. • Haengbangchon Alley • Leeum Art Museum • Itaewon Antique Furniture Street More Itaewon-related tourism content below • Filming locations of the drama Itaewon Class • Go to Itaewon, the most exotic street in Seoul How can I get to Itaewon Street using public transportation? The Itaewon Global Village Festival is Seoul's main global street culture festival where people from all over the world gather and can enjoy unique and various cultures.

description: Gocheok Skydome is the largest capacity stadium in South Korea. In addition to sporting events, arts events such as concerts and awards ceremonies are also often held here. The stadium was completed in September, 2015 and is a cultural sports complex that is open year round. During the baseball season, visitors can watch exciting games and enjoy Korean baseball culture. During the off-season, there are concerts and other cultural events held at Gocheok. The stadium's design is dome-shaped and there are 2 basement levels and 4 above-ground levels. Thanks to its ceiling cover, games and events are unaffected by weather conditions. There are baseball facilities, a swimming pool, gym, soccer field, basketball field and many other facilities open for public use. The stands have 18,000 seats, but for cultural events like concerts, audiences of 20,200 can be accommodated. Gocheok Skydome is the home stadium for the Nexen Heroes from 2016 to 2017. G ocheok Skydome's size makes it one of the largest indoor concert venues in South Korea. The stadium has hosted many K-pop concerts and awards shows such as the KBS Music Awards and more. Frequently Asked Questions about Gocheok Skydome What is the nearest subway station to the Gocheok Sky Dome? The nearest subway station to Gocheok Sky Dome is Guil Station (Subway Line 1). Is there a cafeteria at the Gocheok Sky Dome? There are thirty-two shops inside the Gocheok Sky Dome serving chicken, snack food, and pizza, and a convenience store. Outside, there is a management building with one store, so you can use it when watching baseball. (As of 2024) Can I bring food inside the Gocheok Sky Dome? Bringing food and drinks to the Gocheok Sky Dome may be restricted depending on the nature of the event. Food and beverages in plastic bottles of 1L or less may be brought in during professional baseball games. However, alcoholic drinks, cans, and beverages in glasses are not permitted. In addition, according to Kiwoom Heroes' regulations, food cannot be brought into the stadium when re-entering.

summary: A solo exhibition by Jae-Eun Choi that connects the timeline from the origins of humanity to ecological crisis, calling attention to human responsibility for the destruction of nature and life and to
description: 《Promise (Where Being Be)》 presents the concept of mutual coexistence beyond linguistic meaning, recalling the interconnected solidarity of nature that has traversed time and space long before civilization. Just as the origins of the words promise and bind are intertwined, beings have long been entangled like threads and have existed together through vast stretches of time. Amid rapidly changing global environments, 《Jae-Eun Choi : Promise (Where Being Be)》 asks what kind of life we should aspire to.

name: 《Electric Shock》
summary: An exhibition that traces the sharp relationship between technology and the environment unfolding today through the single circuit of electricity, reexamining the role of art while exploring methods o
description: 《Electric Shock》 is a report on electricity. Electricity, defined as the totality of energy generated through electrons, is a key resource that operates modern society. From household appliances to digital consumption, advanced production lines, and logistics systems, it is difficult to imagine life without electricity. The recent commercialization of artificial intelligence and the expansion of big tech companies have exponentially increased power consumption. Securing and supplying electricity in a stable manner has become a critical issue in rapidly adopting advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence, beginning to determine the competitiveness of nations and corporations. The era of electrical hegemony has arrived, and alongside endless desires for technological advancement, various efforts to develop power within finite resources are underway. Electricity is no longer merely an energy source that enriches daily life but has become an essential weapon that determines survival. This urgency has led to indiscriminate development, turning even efforts for carbon neutrality into romantic promises seen as delaying technological progress. Reflective movements that once called for sustainable coexistence such as posthumanism and the Anthropocene are fading into history already written over the immediate electric war unfolding before us. Electric Shock reveals and traces the sharp relationship between technology and the environment occurring today through a single circuit called electricity.

name: Munassi 《The Season We Fade Away》
summary: A journey that follows the flow of emotions
description: Space K Seoul is pleased to present The Season We Fade Away, a solo exhibition by Moonassi (b. 1980). Rooted in the traditions of Korean painting, the artist has long explored the mind, human relationships, and the subtle inner currents that flow between them. In this exhibition, his paintings serve as both a journey following the flow of emotions and a site for quiet contemplation of the self. For Moonassi, each stroke that remains on paper resembles a ripple spreading across the surface of the mind—like a tremor that gently disturbs still water. Just as the faintest vibration expands into waves, the movements of the inner self—elusive and resistant to words—slowly take shape on the picture plane. The Season We Fade Away reflects on how emotions are born from and fade within relationships. Emotions are awakened and stirred by encounters with others. Like waves on the water, relationships and emotions seep into one another, exchanging light. The artist captures these moments of delicate balance: from figures facing one another, to sharing a gaze toward a single point, to pausing for a breath before a face reflected on the water’s surface. Moonassi does not suppress or define emotions. Instead, he chooses to let them be. This attitude of acceptance becomes a way of seeing the self reflected through others, leading to a quiet observation of one's own being amidst these fluctuations. As suggested by the characters in his name—"Mu (無: non-)" and "Na (我: self)"— his work traverses the boundaries between fullness and emptiness, the self and the other, peering into the space that lies between. In his compositions where the traditional ink meets modern sensibility, emotions do not simply disappear. Rather, they linger, changing form, only to resurface when the time is right. The Season We Fade Away is an exhibition that reflects our own faces on the surface of the water where emotion and relationship intersect. Viewers are invited to accept emotions as they are and, in passing through the tremors of relationships, encounter a quiet moment of return to the self.

name: JEJU HAENYEO : DISAPPEARING WORLDS
summary: An exhibition that reinterprets the ecological and social significance of the Haenyeo culture through experimental works created by artists in collaboration with Haenyeo communities in Jeju.
description: In the summer of 2025, five artists traveled to Jeju. They shared meals with the Haenyeo, sat together at the bulteok, exchanged stories, and observed the tools, discipline, and bodily memories of time. Thus, this exhibition began from two weeks of shared experiences with the Haenyeo. Céline Park examines the hierarchy and silence embedded within the Haenyeo community, Kim Yi-hwa explores the survival of 'nomadic Haenyeo' in the face of climate change, and Moon Su-hyuk critiques how tradition is consumed as a language of capital. Son Ji-min reconsiders the labor of Haenyeo through the lens of femininity and care, while Choi Mi-jin investigates the transmission of knowledge through oral narratives and relationships. 《JEJU HAENYEO: DISAPPEARING WORLDS》 begins in Seoul in November 2025 and continues in Jeju. The Haenyeo, once the mainstay of livelihood, have become symbols of tourism and consumption. Rather than recreating this surface image, the exhibition poses a question: In what forms do the Haenyeo’s bodies, tools, discipline, silence, ecology, and desires persist today, and who is now voicing this legacy anew?

name: Dobong  Kim Sun-young : Solo Exhibition 「Here, Standing on the Star」
summary: The solo exhibition “Here, Standing on a Star” by Kim Sun-young Dobong presents experimental reconstructions of ancient and modern scripts, including oracle bone script and Hangul, within the context
description: Stars are not abstract symbols in the distant sky, they are the very spot where I stand, breathing and living in the present moment. The small tremors and deep immersion we experience in everyday life create a resonance of consciousness, within which a universe, a world, emerges. This exhibition is a condensation of moments deepened and contemplated in prolonged silence and stillness. Time spent alone, detached from relationships, reflects the paths I have walked and the traces of pauses I have taken, while simultaneously serving as a gateway to another world. Within the context of traditional calligraphy, I evoke the primal forms and energies of ancient scripts, especially oracle bone characters, and reconstruct them with Hangul’s formal possibilities through a contemporary sensibility. The characters go beyond mere tools for communication; they manifest as traces of existence and as visual sculptural forms. Letters that breathe like living hearts engrave a pulse into each stroke, leaving trajectories that pierce through time. “Here, Standing on a Star” does not refer to any particular star. It is the “here” where I stand, the moments of now. The characters that bloom in this space transcend personal records and explore how humans perceive and sense the world. I hope this exhibition becomes, for visitors, another star and a pathway to their inner selves. Along this journey, I envision embracing even severed relationships without fear, and standing as a radiant being in one’s own right.

name: Unprecedented Great Flood: The 1925 Eulchuk Year
summary: An exhibition reflecting on this historic disaster on the 100th anniversary of the Great Flood of the Eulchuk Year, with the hope of encouraging collective discussion on future climate change prepared
description: In the summer of 1925, the Han River flood claimed numerous lives and destroyed houses and buildings. The city of Gyeongseong was left isolated with electricity and transportation cut off, and farmlands surrounding the city that sustained its residents were washed away or turned into sand fields. The flood even changed the course of the Han River and erased entire villages. Known as the “Great Flood of the Eulchuk Year,” this disaster had both direct and indirect significant impacts on Seoul. Later, when flood control facilities were installed on the Han River, the flood served as the benchmark, and flood control became a major issue in urban planning. A century later, as continuous flood control efforts have led to floods fading from public memory, the climate crisis has struck. Faced with extreme downpours that have become part of daily life, we are once again reminded of the severity of great floods. On the centennial of the Eulchuk Year Great Flood, this exhibition revisits this historic disaster, serving as an opportunity to collectively consider measures for future climate change preparedness.

description: Since 2017, the Buk-Seoul Museum of Art has been experimenting with flexible communication with audiences through its Vacant Space Project, displaying artworks in spaces other than exhibition halls. The 2025 vacant space exhibition “Sonic Planet – Hertz and Dough” continues this approach, inviting visitors to sense both their own sounds and those of surrounding beings, and to feel the resonance of coexistence. The participating artist team Hertz and Dough is also the first artist group to launch the museum’s “Artist Research” program, which explores the ways in which artistic inquiry and contemplation expand within the creative process. They perceive the world through sound and develop their own narratives by studying the act of listening itself. In the world of sound, where technology and ecology, human and non-human, space and environment intersect, they are asking questions about what and how we hear and understand. The exhibition proposes the following attitudes to create different access points to connect with each other through sound. First, rather than looking for more, close your eyes and listen to the sounds of the here and now. Second, establish listening as an active act rather than mere reception; and third, move beyond an anthropocentric auditory experience to a more sensitive observation of the diverse sounds of the planet. Through these approaches, the soundscape that surrounds us may be transformed into a complex “sonic planet”a sensory field of sound environments.

name: The Boundary Unmade: The Destruction of the Seoul City Wall
summary: An exhibition on the demolition of Hanyangdoseong by Japan and the transformation of Seoul into a colonial city
description: In the second half of 2025, the Hanyangdoseong Museum opens its special exhibition Demolition of Hanyangdoseong, Breaking the Boundaries of Hanyang. King Taejo Yi Seong-gye, founder of the Joseon dynasty, established palaces, the Jongmyo Shrine, and the Sajik Altar in Hanyang based on Confucian ideals, and in 1396 began construction of Hanyangdoseong to defend the capital. The city wall functioned as both a physical boundary separating the capital from the provinces and a symbol of royal authority. After Japan’s victory in the Russo-Japanese War, it began interfering in the Korean Empire, establishing the Wall Disposal Committee in 1907 to commence the full-scale demolition of Hanyangdoseong. Under the pretext of modernization and urban development, gates and walls were destroyed, replaced with colonial government facilities and residential areas. To mark the 80th anniversary of Liberation, this exhibition presents the process of the demolition of Hanyangdoseong by Japan and the transformation of Seoul into a colonial city, using a wide range of historical materials.

summary: Kolon’s cultural and artistic sharing space, Space K Seoul, presents the solo exhibition 《Deep Diver》 by Bae Yun Hwan (b. 1983).
description: Those who dive deep underwater know how to move toward the light. Space K Seoul, Kolon’s cultural and artistic sharing space, hosts the solo exhibition 《Deep Diver》 by Bae Yun Hwan (b. 1983). The artist peels away the familiar layers of light and guides us into the achromatic world of black. That darkness is not emptiness, but rather a space of dense contemplation. His work abandons color and even minimizes form, forcing the gaze inward, deeper and deeper. Just as a diver holds their breath and enters stillness, viewers are invited to halt their thoughts before the canvas, open their senses, and confront its depth. Bae Yun Hwan is an artist who begins with personal experiences and expands his vision to global issues. In his creative process, he unravels not only individual anguish but also the disintegration of communities and the signs of the times such as disasters and wars, expressed through his own allegorical techniques, thereby leading contemporary painting. This exhibition unfolds his narratives more broadly and deeply through works across various genres, including painting, drawing, installation, and video.

name: One Step at a Time: Heehwan Seo, a Master of Hangul Calligraphy
summary: Seoul Arts Center is delighted to present One Step at a Time: Heehwan Seo, a Master of Hangul Calligraphy, an exhibition highlighting the life and art of Pyeongbo Heehwan Seo. Held in commemoration of
description: Seoul Arts Center is delighted to present One Step at a Time: Heehwan Seo, a Master of Hangul Calligraphy, an exhibition highlighting the life and art of Pyeongbo Heehwan Seo. Held in commemoration of the 30th anniversary of Seo’s passing, this large-scale retrospective provides a comprehensive overview of Seo’s extensive oeuvre, spanning works from his early years to his later life. Seo, also known by his art name “Pyeongbo [one step at a time],” was a representative Hangul calligrapher of 20th-century Korea. In 1968, his presentation won the Presidential Award at the 17th National Art Exhibition of Korea, marking the first time a work of calligraphy received this particular honor. Until his death at the age of 61 in 1995, Seo devoted his entire life to exploring Hangul’s calligraphic potential. This incomparable artistic achievement cements his status as an indispensable figure in the history of Korean calligraphy. This exhibition was designed to trace Seo’s journey in achieving the feat of Hangul calligraphy being accepted as an art form. Establishing Hangul calligraphy as an art form — and more importantly, as a calligraphical art — was his lifelong goal, and his perseverance eventually realized this dream. Seo once said, “A turtle in a lake waits a thousand years for its turn to perch atop a lotus leaf,” and his 61-year journey was, indeed, true to his art name, Pyeongbo — one step at a time — in both art and life, advancing step by step without rushing or resting. We hope this exhibition offers visitors an opportunity to deepen their understanding of Seo’s life and art and to keep his memory alive.
